header.name: An Introduction to Quantum Information Theory
header.description:
The course aims to equip students with the prerequisites — mathematical, quantum-mechanical, and information-theoretical — for understanding and further studying, in both academic as well as industry settings, the broad field of quantum information theory and quantum computing. The focus will be on the formal presentation of the various definitions, theorems and proofs, and these will be supplemented with a wide-variety of examples and exercises.

The course is broadly divided into three parts. In the first part, we will cover the necessary mathematical prerequisites followed by the basic postulates of quantum mechanics that serve as the background. We then study the qubit system which is the usual framework of quantum information and computing. We shall then build some of the basics of quantum channels and discuss transformation of states through quantum channels (majorization); these concepts are necessary in the study of quantum communication.

In the second part, we discuss the concept of quantum entanglement, talk about a few tests to distinguish entangled states from the ones that are not entangled (that is, separable states), followed by two essential protocols — the quantum teleportation and superdense coding — which highlight how entanglement allows us to do non-trivial tasks.

In the final part, we discuss information-theoretic concepts. We first briefly introduce the classical Shannon entropy and related cousins, followed by their quantum generalizations (von Neumann entropy). We end the course with a discussion on Shannon's source coding theorem and its quantum analogue — Schumacher's quantum source coding theorem.

If time permits, we would like to discuss quantum nonlocality (for which the Nobel prize in Physics, 2022 was awarded) through the framework of nonlocal games. For that we discuss an example — the CHSH game — which serves as the key component in a variety of quantum communication and information protocols.

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: Students shall be able to identify, describe, and work with quantum states and quantum channels, especially in the case of qubit and two-qubit systems. In addition to these, they shall be able to describe and discuss transformation of states through quantum channels.

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: Students shall be able to appreciate and explain the concept of “entanglement” and will be able to, in simple scenarios, distinguish entangled states from those that are not. Moreover, they shall be able to explain two basic protocols: teleportation and super-dense coding.

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: Students shall be able to compute different entropies of quantum states in simple scenarios.

outcomes.label: CO4
outcomes.raw_text: Students shall be able to understand and describe the CHSH inequality and Bell violation (if quantum nonlocality is covered).

lecture_topics: special types of matrices (hermitian, PSD, isometry, unitary, projection)
Shatten norms and Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
direct sums and tensor products of matrices
Analysis: Euclidean norm, open & closed sets, continuity, convexity in n-dimensional real euclidean space
States (pure states, mixed states, purification of mixed states, Schmidt decomposition, examples)
evolution of a quantum system (optional; if time permits)
Linear maps on the space of matrices
quantum channels (Choi-Kraus representations and Stinesprings representations)
Separability and entanglement: basic properties and examples
a few tests of entanglement (PPT, Entanglement witness)
Classical entroy: Shannon entropy and classical relative entropy
quantum entropy: von Neumann entropy and quantum relative entropy
encoding classical information into quantum states.
Quantum Nonlocality (Special Topic; if time permits)
Nonlocal games: definition, strategies — classical and quantum
the CHSH game: classical bound, quantum violation, quantum bound (Tsirelson’s theorem), non-signalling bound.
